q: Temporary reply queues created per client session are sometimes left behind when clients crash. How can Service Bus remove unused queues automatically?
o: Set AutoDeleteOnIdle on the temporary queues
Set MaxDeliveryCount to 1 on the temporary queues
Enable duplicate detection on the temporary queues
Set the message time-to-live to 1 minute on each queue
e: AutoDeleteOnIdle (the --auto-delete-on-idle parameter) deletes a queue automatically after it has been idle for the configured interval, which suits temporary entities. MaxDeliveryCount, duplicate detection, and message TTL affect messages, not the lifetime of the queue itself.

q: While investigating the dead-letter queue, you want to know why each message ended up there. Where do you look?
o: DeadLetterReason and DeadLetterErrorDescription on each message
The queue's lock duration and MaxDeliveryCount settings
The namespace's Activity log for the time of each failure
Each message's ScheduledEnqueueTime and sequence number
e: When Service Bus or an application dead-letters a message, it records properties such as DeadLetterReason (for example MaxDeliveryCountExceeded or TTLExpiredException) and DeadLetterErrorDescription on the message. Lock duration and scheduling properties don't explain dead-lettering, and the Activity log tracks management operations.

q: A developer accidentally deletes a secret from a key vault that has soft delete enabled with the default settings. What can you do?
o: Recover it; deleted secrets stay recoverable for 90 days by default
Nothing; deletion is permanent even with soft delete enabled
Restore it only from a backup in an Azure Backup vault
Wait for it to reappear automatically after 24 hours
e: Soft delete works like a recycle bin: deleted vaults and objects stay recoverable for a configurable retention period, 90 days by default, and can be recovered or purged during that time. Deletion isn't immediately permanent, no separate backup service is required, and objects don't come back by themselves.

q: Security policy requires that no one, including administrators, can permanently delete secrets before the soft-delete retention period ends. What should you enable?
o: Purge protection
Azure RBAC authorization
A private endpoint
Secret expiration dates
e: Purge protection blocks purging (permanent deletion) of the vault and its objects until the retention period has passed, protecting against malicious insiders. Once enabled it can't be turned off. RBAC controls who can perform actions, private endpoints control network access, and expiration dates don't prevent deletion.

q: You delete a secret named DbPassword in a soft-delete-enabled vault and immediately try to create a new secret with the same name. The request fails with a conflict. Why?
o: The old secret is soft-deleted; recover or purge it first
Secret names can never be reused in the same key vault
The key vault must be restarted before the name is free
You need the Key Vault Secrets User role to create secrets
e: A soft-deleted secret keeps its name reserved until it is recovered or purged (and purging isn't allowed while purge protection is on, until the retention period ends). Names can be reused after purging. Vaults don't restart, and Secrets User only grants read access.

q: A web app's managed identity must only read secret values from a key vault that uses the Azure RBAC permission model. Which role should you assign?
o: Key Vault Secrets User
Key Vault Secrets Officer
Key Vault Contributor
Owner
e: Key Vault Secrets User grants read access to secret contents, which is all the app needs. Secrets Officer can also create, update, and delete secrets. Key Vault Contributor manages the vault resource (management plane) and doesn't grant data access in the RBAC model, and Owner is far too broad.

q: When you create a new key vault, which permission model does Microsoft's guidance use for granting apps and users access?
o: Azure RBAC, with built-in roles such as Key Vault Secrets User
Sharing the vault's access key with each app that needs secrets
Anonymous access restricted by IP address with a firewall rule
A vault password stored in each app's settings and rotated yearly
e: The guidance creates vaults with Azure RBAC authorization enabled (and purge protection) and grants access with built-in data roles. Key Vault has no shared access key or vault password, and anonymous access isn't supported.

q: Which code correctly creates a client to read secrets from the vault contoso-kv in .NET without storing credentials?
o: new SecretClient(new Uri("https://contoso-kv.vault.azure.net"), new DefaultAzureCredential())
new SecretClient("contoso-kv", new ClientSecretCredential("admin", "admin-password"))
new KeyVaultClient("Endpoint=https://contoso-kv.vault.azure.net;AccessKey=<key>")
new SecretClient(new Uri("https://contoso-kv.azurewebsites.net"), new DefaultAzureCredential())
e: SecretClient takes the vault URI (https://<vault-name>.vault.azure.net) and a token credential; DefaultAzureCredential is the recommended passwordless option. Vaults don't have passwords or connection strings, and azurewebsites.net is App Service's domain.

q: The same code uses DefaultAzureCredential on a developer laptop and in an Azure web app. Which identities does it typically use in each place?
o: The developer's Azure CLI or IDE sign-in locally, a managed identity in Azure
The vault's admin access key in both places, read from an environment variable
A hard-coded client secret in both places, stored in appsettings.json
Anonymous access locally and a client certificate in Azure
e: DefaultAzureCredential tries a chain of credential sources: locally it can use the developer's Azure CLI or IDE sign-in, as in the quickstarts, and in Azure it uses the resource's managed identity. That's why the same code works without secrets in both environments.

q: Your code calls GetSecret("ApiKey") without specifying a version. The secret has three versions. Which value is returned?
o: The latest (current) version
The first version ever created
A random version
An error, because the version is required
e: Getting a secret by name without a version returns the latest version of that secret; to read an older one, pass its version identifier. That's why apps that always read the latest version pick up rotated values without code changes.

q: What happens when you call set_secret with an existing secret name and a new value?
o: A new version is created and older versions are kept
The value is overwritten and the old value is lost
The call fails because the secret already exists
A second secret with the same name is created
e: Secrets are versioned: setting a value on an existing name creates a new current version while older versions remain retrievable by version ID. This is what makes rotation and rollback possible. Names stay unique within a vault.

q: A storage account key stored in Key Vault must be rotated automatically without downtime for apps using it. Microsoft's tutorial for resources with two sets of credentials uses which approach?
o: SecretNearExpiry triggers a function that regenerates the unused key as a new version
Delete and recreate the storage account every 90 days with a new key in the vault
A key rotation policy on the secret that regenerates the storage key automatically
A timer function that regenerates both storage keys at the same moment every month
e: For resources with two credentials, the function regenerates the key that isn't currently in use and adds it to Key Vault as a new secret version, so apps keep working with the other key during the switch. The trigger is an Event Grid subscription on SecretNearExpiry. Rotation policies apply to cryptographic keys, and rotating both credentials at once causes downtime.

q: You subscribe a function to the Key Vault SecretNearExpiry event, but it never fires for your API key secret. What is the most likely reason?
o: The secret has no expiration date set
SecretNearExpiry only fires for certificates
The function needs Key Vault Administrator
Event Grid needs a Premium-tier key vault
e: SecretNearExpiry is raised about 30 days before a secret's expiration date, so the secret must have an expiration date (for example set with az keyvault secret set --expires). The event works for secrets, and the function doesn't need vault admin rights to receive events.

q: Which statement about automatic rotation in Azure Key Vault is correct?
o: Keys have rotation policies; secrets need your own rotation logic
Secrets and keys both rotate automatically when they expire
Only certificates can be rotated, through their issuance policy
Rotation always requires deleting the old object first
e: Keys have a rotation policy with lifetime actions (rotate, notify), where the minimum rotation interval is seven days. Secrets don't have a built-in rotation engine, so rotation is implemented with functions or automation reacting to events such as SecretNearExpiry. Rotation creates new versions instead of deleting old ones.

q: You configure a key rotation policy and want an Event Grid notification 30 days before the key expires. What else is required?
o: An expiry time on the policy and an expiration date on the key
A secret with the same name as the key, with its own expiry date
Purge protection disabled on the vault so notifications are allowed
A Premium-tier App Configuration store that forwards the events
e: The notification time in a key rotation policy raises a near-expiry Event Grid event, and it requires an expiry time on the rotation policy and an expiration date on the key. Secrets, purge protection settings, and App Configuration aren't part of this.

q: An app retrieves secrets in a hot code path, and calls to Key Vault occasionally fail with transient errors. Which client configuration does the tutorial show?
o: An exponential retry policy in SecretClientOptions
A new SecretClient for every request to Key Vault
TLS disabled on the client to reduce latency
Anonymous access so that no token is requested
e: The tutorial configures SecretClientOptions.Retry with exponential mode, delays, and a maximum number of retries so transient failures are retried safely. Creating clients per request adds overhead, and disabling TLS or using anonymous access isn't possible or safe. Caching secret values in the app also reduces calls.

q: Your application must sign tokens with an RSA private key, and the private key must never leave Key Vault. Which object type should you store?
o: A key, signing through the Key Vault keys API
A secret that contains the PEM private key
An App Configuration key-value with the key
An environment variable in App Service
e: Key Vault keys support cryptographic operations such as sign and decrypt inside the service, so the private key material isn't returned to the app. Storing the PEM as a secret means the app downloads the private key. App Configuration and environment variables aren't designed for private key protection.

q: You need RSA keys protected by a hardware security module (RSA-HSM) for customer-managed key encryption. What does this require in Key Vault?
o: The Premium tier of Key Vault
The Standard tier with soft delete disabled
Any tier, because all keys are HSM-backed
A Basic tier vault
e: RSA-HSM keys are only available in the Premium tier of Key Vault; Standard vaults use software-protected keys. Soft delete settings don't affect key protection type, and Key Vault has no Basic tier.

q: An app stores a JSON object with several values as a single Key Vault secret. What must the app do?
o: Serialize it to a string (such as JSON) and deserialize it on read
Nothing, because Key Vault stores native JSON objects as secrets
Split it into Key Vault keys, one key for each JSON property
Store it as a certificate so that the structure is preserved
e: A secret value is a string. The JavaScript developer guide notes that you must serialize values such as JSON or Base64 data before setting them and deserialize them after retrieval. Keys are for cryptographic material, and certificates are for X.509 certificates.

q: You must load a TLS certificate, including its private key, that is stored in Key Vault. How can the app retrieve the full certificate with the private key?
o: Read it as a secret; the key pair is stored as a secret
Read it from the keys endpoint, which returns the private key
Read it from the certificates endpoint, which includes the private key
It can't be retrieved; certificates with private keys stay in the vault
e: Key Vault stores a certificate's public and private key pair as a secret with the same name, so an app can retrieve the full certificate through the secrets API. The certificates endpoint returns the public certificate and metadata, and the keys endpoint doesn't return private key material.

q: In the JavaScript SDK, which statement about deleting a secret is correct?
o: beginDeleteSecret returns a poller for a long-running delete
deleteSecret deletes the secret synchronously and permanently
Deleting a secret also deletes the vault if it's the last one
You can only delete secrets in the Azure portal, not the SDK
e: Deletion is a long-running operation in the SDK: beginDeleteSecret returns a poller that completes when the secret is deleted (moved to the soft-deleted state in a soft-delete-enabled vault). It doesn't permanently purge the secret or affect the vault, and SDKs and the CLI can delete secrets.

q: A Python app sets a secret and then reads it back. Which library and class does the quickstart use?
o: azure-keyvault-secrets with SecretClient and DefaultAzureCredential
azure-storage-blob with BlobClient and an account key
azure-appconfiguration with AzureAppConfigurationClient
requests with the vault's admin password in a header
e: The Python quickstart uses SecretClient from azure-keyvault-secrets with a vault URL and DefaultAzureCredential from azure-identity, then calls set_secret and get_secret. The other libraries target Blob storage and App Configuration, and Key Vault has no admin password.

q: A secret's properties show recoveryLevel Recoverable+Purgeable and recoverableDays 90. What do these tell you?
o: Recoverable for 90 days after deletion, and purgeable meanwhile
The secret expires automatically 90 days after it was created
The secret can only be read 90 times before it's disabled
The secret will be rotated automatically every 90 days
e: recoverableDays is the number of days a deleted secret can be recovered, and the recovery level describes the protection: Recoverable+Purgeable means soft delete is on but purge protection isn't, so it can be purged before the period ends. These properties don't describe expiry, read limits, or rotation.

q: Container apps, functions, and VMs in your solution all need the same set of Key Vault permissions, and you want one identity you can grant once and reuse. Which kind of managed identity fits?
o: A user-assigned managed identity attached to each resource
A system-assigned identity, which can be shared across resources
The Key Vault's own identity
A personal Microsoft account
e: A user-assigned managed identity is a standalone resource that can be attached to multiple Azure resources, so one role assignment covers them all; system-assigned identities are tied to a single resource's lifecycle. The vault's identity and personal accounts aren't meant for app access.

q: The key AppName:DbEndpoint must have different values for Test, Staging, and Production in one App Configuration store. How should you model this?
o: The same key with labels Test, Staging, and Production
Three stores, each with its own copy of the key
The environment name appended to every value
Feature flags named after each environment
e: Labels differentiate key-values that share a key, and a common use is one label per environment. Apps select the label they need while key names in code stay the same. Separate stores add management overhead, encoding environments in values is error-prone, and feature flags are for toggling functionality.

q: A .NET app calls AddAzureAppConfiguration with default options. New keys added with the label dev don't appear in the app. Why?
o: By default only unlabeled keys load; select the dev label explicitly
Labels can't be read by .NET apps through the configuration provider
The app needs the App Configuration Data Owner role to read labels
New keys are only visible to apps 24 hours after they're created
e: The .NET provider loads key-values without a label unless you specify selectors, so keys labeled dev are ignored until you select that label (for example by selecting keys with labels null and dev). Read access only needs Data Reader, and keys are visible immediately.

q: An app must pick up configuration changes without restarting, but you want to avoid inconsistent states while several keys are being edited and keep requests to the store low. What does Microsoft recommend?
o: Watch one sentinel key, update it last, and refresh all keys when it changes
Poll every key individually every second and apply changes as they arrive
Restart the app after every change so it always loads a complete set
Store all configuration in one large JSON key and poll it constantly
e: A sentinel key is updated after you finish changing the other keys. The provider monitors only the sentinel and reloads everything when it changes, which keeps configuration consistent and reduces requests to the store. Polling every key frequently adds load and can load half-finished changes.

q: You configured dynamic refresh in ASP.NET Core with ConfigureRefresh and a sentinel key, but the app never sees updates. What is a likely missing piece?
o: Refresh must be triggered, such as by the middleware or TryRefreshAsync
The sentinel key must be deleted after each update to signal a change
The app must use access keys instead of Entra ID for refresh to work
Dynamic refresh only works in Python and JavaScript, not in .NET apps
e: ConfigureRefresh tells the provider what to watch and how long values are cached, but it doesn't refresh on every read; refresh runs when the middleware (UseAzureAppConfiguration) or your code calls TryRefreshAsync. Deleting the sentinel isn't the pattern, and authentication type and language don't change this.

q: A controller reads settings through IOptions<Settings>, and it never shows updated values even though refresh is configured. What should you change?
o: Use IOptionsSnapshot<T> or IOptionsMonitor<T> instead
Use a static variable that is set once at startup
Restart the app every minute to reload the settings
Store the settings in Key Vault instead of App Configuration
e: The dynamic configuration tutorial notes that IOptions<T> doesn't read configuration data after the app has started, so it can't reflect refreshed values; IOptionsSnapshot<T> (per request) or IOptionsMonitor<T> do. Static variables and scheduled restarts are workarounds, and Key Vault isn't the fix here.

q: You toggle a feature flag in App Configuration. With default settings in the ASP.NET Core quickstart, how soon does the app see the change?
o: Within about 30 seconds
Immediately, on the next request
Only after the app restarts
After the 24-hour cache expires
e: The default refresh interval for feature flags is 30 seconds, configurable through feature flag options, so the app picks up the change without restarting or redeploying. It isn't instant, and 24 hours is the App Service Key Vault reference cache, not App Configuration feature flags.

q: An app needs a database password and other settings. How should you combine App Configuration and Key Vault?
o: Keep it in Key Vault, add a Key Vault reference in App Configuration
Store the password directly as an App Configuration value
Store all settings in Key Vault and drop App Configuration
Put the password in a feature flag with a filter
e: App Configuration can hold Key Vault references: it stores the secret's URI rather than its value, and the provider uses the app's credentials to fetch the secret from Key Vault. The app's identity therefore needs read access to the secret too. Best practice is to keep secrets in Key Vault, not as plain configuration values.

q: A secret referenced from App Configuration is rotated in Key Vault, but the app keeps using the old value. How can the .NET provider pick up rotated secrets without restarting?
o: Set a secret refresh interval (SetSecretRefreshInterval)
Change the label of the Key Vault reference after each rotation
Set the feature flag refresh interval to 0 so everything reloads
Delete and recreate the App Configuration store after rotation
e: The provider caches resolved Key Vault secrets. Setting a secret refresh interval makes it reload secrets and certificates from Key Vault periodically, so rotated values are picked up automatically. Relabeling keys or changing feature flag refresh doesn't affect secret caching.

q: An application only reads configuration from App Configuration using Microsoft Entra ID. Which role should its identity have?
o: App Configuration Data Reader
App Configuration Reader
App Configuration Data Owner
Reader on the subscription
e: App Configuration Data Reader grants read access to the data plane (key-values, snapshots, feature flags). App Configuration Reader is a control-plane role that reads the resource but not its data, Data Owner adds write and delete, and subscription Reader doesn't grant data access.

q: You want to deploy a new set of configuration changes safely, test it, and be able to roll back to a known-good set instantly. Which App Configuration feature helps most?
o: Snapshots: immutable point-in-time sets of key-values
A longer sentinel refresh interval during deployments
Longer key names that include the release version
Disabling labels so only one value exists per key
e: Snapshots capture a consistent, immutable set of configuration that you can build and test before production and progressively roll out, keeping last-known-good snapshots for rollback. Refresh intervals, key names, and labels alone don't give an immutable versioned set.

q: A multitenant app stores per-tenant settings in one App Configuration store and also needs environment variations. What does the Azure Architecture Center recommend?
o: Key prefixes for tenants; labels kept for environments
The tenant ID as the label for every key in the store
One store per environment and one label per tenant
Tenant settings stored as feature flags with filters
e: If tenant IDs become labels, labels can't be used for anything else, so the guidance suggests key prefixes for tenant-specific settings and labels for purposes such as environments or versions. Feature flags are for turning features on and off.

q: A Python console app should reload settings when a key named sentinel changes. Which provider API does the tutorial use?
o: load(...) with refresh_on=[WatchKey("sentinel")], then refresh()
os.environ["sentinel"], checked in a loop every few seconds
SecretClient from azure-keyvault-secrets, watching the key
A timer that re-imports the settings module every minute
e: The Python provider's load function accepts refresh options, including WatchKey for the sentinel; calling refresh checks the sentinel and reloads all values if it changed. Environment variables and Key Vault clients don't watch App Configuration, and re-importing modules isn't the provider's mechanism.

q: Your AKS workloads read configuration from Kubernetes ConfigMaps, and you want those ConfigMaps populated and refreshed from Azure App Configuration without changing app code. What should you use?
o: The Azure App Configuration Kubernetes Provider
An ACR task
Container insights
A Kubernetes CronJob that runs kubectl edit
e: The App Configuration Kubernetes Provider runs in the cluster and generates ConfigMaps (and Secrets for Key Vault references) from an App Configuration store, with optional periodic refresh. ACR tasks build images, Container insights collects logs and metrics, and manual kubectl edits aren't automated or reliable.

q: Your App Configuration store has replicas in two regions. How do the App Configuration providers use them by default?
o: They discover replicas automatically and fail over to them
They ignore replicas unless you list each one in code
They write to every replica each time they read a value
They can't read from replicas, which exist only for backups
e: Replica discovery is on by default in the providers (replicaDiscoveryEnabled defaults to true in the Kubernetes provider), so clients discover replicas and use them for failover, and load balancing across replicas can also be enabled. Replicas serve reads, and providers don't write on reads.

q: A JavaScript app calls load() from the App Configuration provider without options. Which key-values are loaded?
o: All key-values that have no label
All key-values with every label
Only feature flags
Only keys that start with the app name
e: By default the JavaScript provider's load method loads all configuration with no label. Use selectors in the options (key filter and label filter) to load other labels or limit keys, and enable feature flags separately.

q: How does the ASP.NET Core quickstart connect to App Configuration without storing a connection string?
o: options.Connect(new Uri(endpoint), new DefaultAzureCredential())
options.Connect(builder.Configuration["AppConfig:PrimaryAccessKey"])
options.Connect(new Uri(endpoint)) with anonymous access enabled
A Key Vault reference in appsettings.json that points to the store
e: The provider can connect with the store endpoint and a token credential such as DefaultAzureCredential, which avoids connection strings; the identity needs App Configuration Data Reader (or Owner for writes). Access keys are secrets to manage, and stores don't allow anonymous reads.

q: How should you reference a key-value that explicitly has no label when querying App Configuration through its REST API?
o: Use \0, URL-encoded as %00
Use the label value default
Leave out the label parameter
Use an asterisk (*) as the label
e: By default a key-value has no label; to explicitly select key-values without a label, use \0 (URL-encoded as %00). default is just a normal label name, and an asterisk matches any label rather than no label.

q: Which data does Microsoft recommend keeping outside App Configuration, referencing it from elsewhere if needed?
o: Secrets and large files
Feature flags and their filters
Environment-specific endpoints
Logging levels per component
e: App Configuration is meant for configuration you would otherwise put in files or environment variables. The best practices article suggests storing secrets in Key Vault, files in Azure Storage, and similar data in their natural stores, while feature flags, endpoints, and log levels fit App Configuration well.

q: You add the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro to an ASP.NET Core app. Which two steps send traces, metrics, and logs to Application Insights? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.
o: Call AddOpenTelemetry().UseAzureMonitor() in Program.cs
Set APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING for the app
Set the instrumentation key in web.config under appSettings
Install the classic Application Insights SDK next to the distro
e: Enabling the distro means adding UseAzureMonitor() and supplying the connection string, typically through the APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING environment variable. Instrumentation keys alone are legacy, and installing the classic SDK next to the distro isn't needed and can duplicate telemetry.

q: Where should production apps get the Application Insights connection string when using the OpenTelemetry Distro?
o: From an environment variable, not hard-coded
Hard-coded in the source code for every build
From a query string parameter on each request
From the user's browser cookies on each page
e: Microsoft recommends setting the connection string in code only for local development and test; for production, use an environment variable, or a configuration file for Java. That keeps environment-specific values out of builds and lets you change them without redeploying.

q: You upgrade from the Application Insights .NET SDK 2.x to 3.x, which is built on OpenTelemetry. The app configured only an instrumentation key. What must you change?
o: Provide a connection string; 3.x requires one
Nothing; the instrumentation key alone still works
Add adaptive sampling settings to the configuration
Remove all telemetry configuration from the app
e: The migration guide says to use TelemetryConfiguration.ConnectionString instead of an instrumentation key; SDK 3.x requires a connection string and can fail at startup if it isn't configured. Adaptive sampling is replaced by other sampling options, and removing configuration stops telemetry.

q: Telemetry volume from a busy Node.js service is too high. Using the Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro, how do you keep about 10 percent of traces?
o: samplingRatio 0.1 with tracesPerSecond 0
Set the log level to Error for all loggers
Delete and recreate the Application Insights resource
Set maxDeliveryAttempts to 10 in the exporter
e: The distro supports fixed-percentage sampling with samplingRatio and rate-limited sampling with tracesPerSecond; the documented example keeps about 10 percent of traces with samplingRatio 0.1 and tracesPerSecond 0. Log levels affect logs, not trace sampling, and maxDeliveryAttempts is an Event Grid setting.

q: With sampling enabled in several microservices, you worry that a trace will be kept in one service but dropped in another. How does Application Insights reduce this risk?
o: It samples on a hash of the trace ID, so decisions match
Every service always keeps 100 percent of dependencies
Sampling is disabled automatically for distributed traces
Upstream services send a flag that downstream services obey
e: Application Insights samples based on a hash of the trace ID to keep traces complete, so services sampling at the same rate make consistent decisions for a given trace. The FAQ notes that upstream sampling decisions in W3C headers don't drive the downstream decision; the trace ID hash does.

q: With OpenTelemetry and Application Insights, in which tables are distributed tracing spans stored?
o: requests and dependencies
traces only
customEvents only
exceptions and pageViews
e: Spans for distributed tracing are stored in the requests and dependencies tables (AppRequests and AppDependencies in Log Analytics). Application log records go to the traces table for legacy reasons. customEvents, exceptions, and pageViews hold other telemetry types.

q: You need to find every telemetry item (requests, dependencies, logs) that belongs to one end-to-end transaction across services. Which field ties them together?
o: operation_Id (the W3C trace-id)
cloud_RoleInstance of the frontend
client_IP of the original caller
itemCount on the first request
e: Every telemetry item in a distributed trace shares the same operation_Id, which Application Insights maps from the W3C trace-id; the transaction diagnostics view shows all telemetry with that Operation ID. Role instance, client IP, and item count don't identify a transaction.

q: In the W3C Trace Context standard used by OpenTelemetry, what identifies the overall transaction and what identifies an individual operation within it?
o: A 16-byte trace-id and an 8-byte span-id
An 8-byte trace-id and a 16-byte span-id
A GUID session ID and a sequence number
The HTTP request ID and the thread ID
e: Each trace gets a globally unique 16-byte trace-id, and each activity within it gets a unique 8-byte span-id. These travel between services in the traceparent header so each service can continue the same trace.

q: In the Application Map, all your services appear under one confusing name. How do you give each service its own cloud role name with OpenTelemetry?
o: Set service.name (for example OTEL_SERVICE_NAME) per service
Use a separate Application Insights resource per HTTP route
Rename the Log Analytics workspace to match each service
Add a custom metric named role with the service's name
e: Application Insights maps the OpenTelemetry resource attributes service.name (with service.namespace) to the cloud role name, and service.instance.id to the role instance. Setting them per service, for example through OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, makes the map show distinct components.

q: A Java service uses the Application Insights Java agent built on OpenTelemetry. You want a business method to appear as its own span with minimal code. What is the simplest option?
o: Annotate the method with @WithSpan
Write a log line at the start and end of the method
Create a custom metric
Add the method name to the connection string
e: The simplest way to add your own spans in Java is OpenTelemetry's @WithSpan annotation, and spans populate the requests and dependencies tables. Log lines become traces rather than spans, metrics aggregate numbers, and the connection string only identifies the destination.

q: You must add a property such as tenantId to every span before it is exported to Application Insights. Which OpenTelemetry extensibility point fits?
o: A span processor registered with the distro
A KQL function applied in the workspace
An Event Grid filter on the telemetry topic
A log processor that rewrites span names
e: Span processors hook into span start and end and can add or modify attributes before export; the migration guide shows registering one with the distro to add a custom property. KQL runs at query time and can't change stored telemetry, and Event Grid filters and scale rules are unrelated.

q: Health-check requests to /healthz flood Application Insights. How can you stop collecting them with OpenTelemetry?
o: Configure the HTTP instrumentation to exclude them
Delete them in Log Analytics every day with a job
Lower the sampling ratio to 0 for the whole service
Disable the Application Insights resource at night
e: The filtering guide shows configuring instrumentation libraries (such as the HTTP instrumentation) to ignore specific incoming requests, so they are never recorded. Deleting data afterward doesn't stop ingestion costs, a sampling ratio of 0 drops everything, and disabling the resource stops all monitoring.

q: In a Node.js app, the Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro is initialized after Express and the database client are imported, and outgoing calls aren't tracked. What should you change?
o: Initialize the distro before loading app libraries
Initialize it after the first request is handled
Use a different Application Insights resource
Increase the sampling ratio to 1.0 for the app
e: Instrumentation must be enabled before the libraries it instruments are loaded; the guidance for Node.js says to enable it first, and ESM apps must preload the distro loader. Initializing later, changing resources, or changing sampling doesn't fix missing instrumentation.

q: A project already initializes the Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro, and a teammate adds the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro initialization as well. What does Microsoft advise?
o: Don't initialize both distros together; use one
Initialize both to get double coverage
Initialize the Azure Monitor Distro first, then the Microsoft distro
It doesn't matter, because they share state
e: The configuration guidance states that the Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro and the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro shouldn't be initialized together; Azure Monitor stays the destination with a single distro. Running both risks duplicate or conflicting pipelines.

q: Your .NET app used EnableAdaptiveSampling in the classic Application Insights SDK. After moving to the OpenTelemetry-based SDK 3.x, what replaces it?
o: TracesPerSecond or SamplingRatio
Event Grid retry policies
KQL sample operators in queries
The functionTimeout setting
e: The migration guide maps EnableAdaptiveSampling to the OpenTelemetry-based options TracesPerSecond (rate-limited) or SamplingRatio (fixed percentage). KQL sample operators only affect query results, and the other settings belong to other services.

q: You want to record the distribution of order processing times (for percentiles) as a custom metric with OpenTelemetry. Which instrument fits?
o: A histogram from a Meter
A counter from a Meter
A span attribute on each order
A log message per order
e: Histograms record value distributions, which Application Insights can aggregate into percentiles; the add-and-modify guide includes a histogram example using the metrics API. Counters only add up values, and span attributes or log messages aren't aggregated as metrics.

q: An OpenTelemetry span has kind CLIENT, for example an outgoing HTTP call to a payment API. In which Application Insights table does it appear?
o: dependencies
requests
pageViews
availabilityResults
e: Spans that represent incoming work (SERVER and CONSUMER kinds) become requests, while outgoing or internal work (CLIENT, PRODUCER, and INTERNAL kinds) becomes dependencies. pageViews and availabilityResults come from browser telemetry and availability tests.

q: A Java app gets its Application Insights connection string from a system property, an environment variable, and a configuration file, each with a different value. Which one wins?
o: System property, then environment variable, then file
The configuration file always wins over the others
The environment variable always wins over the others
Whichever source the agent happens to read last
e: For Java, the documented precedence when the connection string is set in more than one place is: system property, then environment variable, then configuration file. Knowing the order prevents surprises when environments set it in different ways.

q: You want an Azure Functions app (v4) to emit its host and worker telemetry using OpenTelemetry. Which host.json setting is shown in Microsoft's migration guidance?
o: "telemetryMode": "OpenTelemetry"
"functionTimeout": "OpenTelemetry"
"logging": "none"
"extensionBundle": "OpenTelemetry"
e: Setting telemetryMode to OpenTelemetry in host.json switches the Functions host to emit OpenTelemetry-based telemetry, which you then export to Application Insights or another OTLP destination. functionTimeout controls execution time, and the other values aren't valid settings for this.

q: In Application Insights, you open one failed request and want to see the full end-to-end chain of calls across services with timings. Which experience should you use?
o: Transaction diagnostics
Live metrics only
The Activity log
Azure Advisor
e: The transaction diagnostics experience shows all telemetry of a single operation, sharing one Operation ID, as a timeline across components. Live metrics shows real-time aggregates, the Activity log records management operations, and Advisor gives recommendations.
